title: Dance steps then and now: two-step, one-step, the Castles
summary: He describes intricate close-contact two-step and one-step dancing, Irene Castle dancing to Piron's band at the St. Charles, and how dancing differs today.

story.theme_name: Playing for dancers: dance bands and the dances themselves
story.community_name: Dancing to the band: quadrilles, waltzes and dance sets

blocks.x: Once, one or fewer, the younger people would. But the only dance that they had then at the time was the two-step, but that became extremely intricate. The steps had developed along with that. And it was not because the, what do you call them, the castles came. Irene Castle and Osborne came and played at the St. Charles. Had a very fine place upstairs. Piran was a band, and they danced, the castles danced to them. But that didn't influence the dancing that we did. We were moving along. Who brought it in, I don't know, but it became very intricate steps. A great deal of turning and twisting and side steps and all that would be very difficult for the kids, even though they are good dancers today. It would be very difficult for them to do that. And, let's see, can you stop it a minute? It looks like you're running out. Yeah. You got enough room? The dancing today is, if you'll notice, is with the people with their bodies apart, not touching. But on the contrary, when we were dancing, you had direct body contact with a grip all the way around the girl. And not for a sexual reason, although there were some that would get over in the corner and roll it, you know. But what they did was to, those steps had to be perfect between the couples or it wouldn't go. And, as I say, very rapid, intricate changes of steps. It became first the two steps, then the one step. But we didn't do the Charleston and those as a group very much. A few people did it for frills and that's about all.
They did have a dancing school. Mm-hm.
